 Indonesia Cuts Gas Exports to Singapore: Energy Security, Diplomatic Tensions, and the Haze Crisis
 The Supply Reduction Targeted Cuts and Their Scale Domestic Priorities Haze, Rhetoric, and Rising Diplomatic Heat A Critical Energy Partnership Under Strain Wider Regional Implications Uncertain Days Ahead
 By Mark Lim Published about 9 hours ago • 3 min read Photo by KWON JUNHO on Unsplash Indonesia has moved to curtail natural gas exports to Singapore, effective Saturday, in a decision framed as essential to safeguarding domestic energy reliability but arriving amid escalating public friction over transboundary air pollution and forest fires. The cut of roughly 8% of Indonesia’s total gas shipments to Singapore marks a significant shift in a long-standing energy relationship and underscores how environmental crises can rapidly spill over into trade and diplomacy.
 The Supply Reduction
 Djoko Siswanto, head of Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas, confirmed the move, stating that a combined 31 million standard cubic feet per day would be withheld from Singapore. The reduction is split between two key producing regions: 15 million standard cubic feet per day from the Natuna fields in the Riau Islands, and 16 million standard cubic feet per day from Sumatra. Djoko emphasised the core rationale: “to maintain the reliability of domestic gas supply for electricity.” He added that the situation would be “monitored on a daily basis,” indicating the measure may be adjusted or extended depending on conditions. For now, Singapore is the only recipient affected.
 Targeted Cuts and Their Scale
 The numbers carry tangible weight. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Indonesia supplied Singapore with 145.3 billion cubic feet of natural gas in 2024 , making it one of the city-state’s most important energy partners. The newly announced cut represents approximately 8% of that annual volume a meaningful reduction that will require Singapore to seek alternative supplies or adjust its power generation profile. As of this writing, the Singapore government has not issued an official response.
 Domestic Priorities
 Indonesian authorities have positioned the decision as a straightforward matter of national necessity. Ensuring stable gas flow to domestic power plants is critical amid growing demand, seasonal shifts in consumption, and infrastructure constraints. The move was foreshadowed just two days earlier, on Thursday, when Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia stated publicly that he was considering export curbs to prioritise local needs. His remarks carried an added edge: he also warned Jakarta would take action against countries that “do not respect” Indonesia, linking energy policy to broader regional tensions.
 Haze, Rhetoric, and Rising Diplomatic Heat
 The dual messaging, practical and defensive reflects a deeply strained regional atmosphere. For months, Indonesia has battled widespread forest and land fires that have consumed more than 1.9 million hectares in the nine months through September, according to monitoring group Nusantara Atlas. The resulting haze has blanketed cities across Malaysia, Singapore, and East Timor, pushing air quality into hazardous ranges and prompting health alerts across the region.
 Singapore has signalled it intends to pursue legal action against companies linked to the fires, a stance that has drawn sharp pushback in Jakarta. On Wednesday, President Prabowo Subianto publicly reproached “countries that like to insult” Indonesia over the crisis, without naming specific nations directly. The convergence of energy export decisions with this rhetoric has raised questions over whether the two matters are being deliberately intertwined and whether economic tools are becoming part of the diplomatic response.
 A Critical Energy Partnership Under Strain
 For Singapore, Indonesia’s gas supplies have long been a cornerstone of energy security, providing a steady, geographically close source of fuel for power generation. Any sustained reduction carries implications for electricity costs, reserve margins, and the pace of transition toward other energy sources. For Indonesia, balancing export revenue against domestic needs is a perennial challenge made sharper by rising consumption, infrastructure gaps, and the political imperative to keep power affordable and reliable at home. Whether the cut is driven purely by technical supply constraints or carries an element of diplomatic signalling, the practical effect is the same: a tested bilateral relationship faces new stress.
 Wider Regional Implications
 The episode also reverberates beyond the two nations. Malaysia and other ASEAN members have endured weeks of poor air quality and public pressure to address the haze, prompting the regional bloc to schedule an emergency meeting on the crisis. If resource decisions become entangled in cross-border disputes, other areas of cooperation, trade, investment, and environmental governance could face ripple effects. How Jakarta and Singapore manage this moment may set precedents for how ASEAN addresses overlapping interests in energy, environment, and sovereignty.
 Uncertain Days Ahead
 For now, Indonesia says it will review gas volumes daily, leaving open the possibility of restoration or further cuts. Singapore has yet to indicate how it will bridge the supply gap. What is clear is that two persistent regional challenges energy security and environmental stewardship, have collided. Resolving them will require separating legitimate domestic needs from political rhetoric, rebuilding trust across borders, and addressing the root causes of the fires themselves. Until then, the haze hangs over more than just the skies.
